summary: Describes using BGP as a control plane for service function chaining. It introduces a new BGP address family with two route types, one for a node to advertise that it hosts a service function and another for advertising the chain.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP, the Internet's directions system, is taught to also share which stations offer which services and the order traffic should visit them.

questions: bgp control plane for service function chaining
what is a service function path route
subtitle: How BGP can tell a network which service functions exist and in what order packets should visit them.

tldr.problem: Service function chains (firewalls, load balancers and the like applied in a set order) used to depend on where the boxes sat in the network topology, which made chains hard to change and hard to make redundant.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9015 adds a BGP address family (AFI 31, SAFI 9) with two route types: one where a node advertises a service function instance it hosts, and one where a controller advertises a whole path of functions with a Service Path Identifier for use in the Network Service Header.
tldr.outcome: Forwarders and classifiers can be programmed with chains over BGP, with choices among instances, bidirectional paths, loops, jumps and branches. It is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted.

today: RFC 9015 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2021, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the NSH of RFC 8300 and the architecture of RFC 7665.

sections.title: Why Chains Need a Control Plane
sections.content:
Delivering an end-to-end service can require a packet to pass through a series of service functions (SFs), such as WAN and application accelerators, Deep Packet Inspection engines, firewalls, TCP optimizers and server load balancers, in a specified order. This is called service function chaining.

Historically, the nodes hosting those functions were placed in the topology so that a packet could not reach its destination without passing through all of them in order. The RFC says this limited how well a chain could adapt to link or node failures, network utilization or offered load. Configuring a chain was operationally complex, redundant functions had to be co-located with the primary ones, and bidirectional chains were hard to support with simple routing when forwarding was asymmetric.

The SFC architecture of RFC 7665 instead builds chains in their own overlay network over a common underlay. RFC 9015 supplies the missing control plane for that architecture, using BGP, for use with the Network Service Header of RFC 8300.
sections.plainLanguage: Long ago, to make sure a package went through the right stations, the stations had to sit along the only road. This RFC lets the stations be anywhere and sends the package along a list of stops instead.

sections.title: The Building Blocks
sections.content:
A Service Function Chain (SFC) is an ordered list of service functions. A Service Function Path (SFP) says which instances of those functions are acceptable. In the Network Service Header (NSH), the Service Path Identifier (SPI) is a 24-bit number naming an SFP, and the Service Index (SI) is an 8-bit number marking a point in that path.

A classifier sits at each ingress to the overlay. It assigns a packet flow to an SFP, sets the SPI, sets the SI to the first hop, and prepends the NSH. A Service Function Forwarder (SFF) receives packets, strips the encapsulation, hands the packet and NSH to the service function instance (SFI), and picks the next hop when the packet comes back. The SFI itself has no knowledge of the SFP. A controller plans the SFPs and tells the control plane and classifiers what to do.

The RFC adds the Service Function Type (SFT), a category such as firewall, held in an IANA registry. One SFF can support several types, and several instances of each, which allows load balancing and redundancy. The RFC notes that RFC 8300 is intended for use within a single provider's operational domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A path is a numbered list of stops. A guide at the door writes the list number and the first stop on the package. At each stop, a helper does a job and the package goes on to the next number.

sections.title: The Two Route Types
sections.content:
The new address family is carried in BGP with the Multiprotocol Extensions, using AFI 31 and SAFI 9. The NLRI starts with a 2-octet Route Type and a 2-octet Length, followed by type-specific data. Two speakers MUST confirm support through BGP capabilities advertisements, and the next hop MUST be a loopback address of the advertising SFF.

The Service Function Instance Route (SFIR, type 1) holds an 8-octet Route Distinguisher and a 2-octet Service Function Type. A node hosting service functions MUST originate an SFIR for each type it hosts and MAY advertise one per instance. The update MUST carry a tunnel encapsulation attribute from RFC 9012, which tells others how to reach the instance. Optional extended communities (type 0x0b) mark SFIR pools (sub-type 1) and MPLS label pairs (sub-type 2).

The Service Function Path Route (SFPR, type 2) holds an 8-octet Route Distinguisher and a 3-octet SPI. The path itself is described in a new optional transitive BGP path attribute, the SFP attribute (type code 37), built from TLVs: optional Association TLVs, and one or more Hop TLVs, each with an SI and SFT Sub-TLVs listing acceptable instances by their SFIR route distinguishers. A route distinguisher of zero means any instance of that type. The attribute follows the error handling of RFC 7606, with several malformed cases treated as withdraw.
sections.plainLanguage: One kind of note says here is a helper and how to reach it. The other kind says here is a numbered trip and the stops, in order, with which helpers are allowed at each stop.

sections.title: How Routes Drive Forwarding
sections.content:
Route Targets, as in RFC 4364, let several service function overlay networks (or VPN instances) share one network. Every SFIR and SFPR carries one or more route targets, and each node imports only matching routes. An SFF builds forwarding state only for the SFPs on which it appears.

When an SFF imports an SFPR, it looks for its own SFIR route distinguishers (or a zero) in the path. For each occurrence it creates state mapping the SPI and SI of incoming packets to local instances, and state for sending packets onward after the instance has processed them. If several local instances match, local policy such as load balancing picks one.

SI values run from 255 down to 1 and MUST be monotonically decreasing and appear only once, but gaps are allowed so that a function can be inserted or removed without renumbering. If a received SI is not in the path, the SFF SHOULD reduce it to the next smaller SI present, and if none exists the SI is treated as not valid as in RFC 8300.

If two SFPRs share an SPI but have different route distinguishers, the SFF MUST use the one with the numerically lowest distinguisher and SHOULD log it. A controller that wants to change a path is RECOMMENDED to use a new SPI, and SHOULD NOT reuse a withdrawn SPI until a configurable timer has passed, with a default of one hour.
sections.plainLanguage: Each station only remembers the trips that include it. When a package arrives with a trip number and stop number, the station knows which helper to give it to, and where it goes next.

sections.title: Choosing Among Instances
sections.content:
After an instance returns a packet, the SPI and SI may leave the SFF with a choice of next-hop types and instances. The SFF MUST choose one, identify the SFF that supports it, and send the packet there. Choices may be for load balancing, or to distinguish actions, for example sending admitted packets onward but diverting suspect packets to a penalty box.

The SFF finds the relevant SFIRs: those with the matching route target, a matching SFT, and either a matching route distinguisher, a zero entry (any instance of that type), or membership in a listed pool. It then picks according to local policy, typically the nearest instances in the underlay with load balancing among them. An instance may pass back hints that influence the choice.

If no relevant instance remains, the SFPR is unusable, and the originating controller SHOULD withdraw it or re-advertise it with new route distinguishers for that hop.
sections.plainLanguage: When there are several helpers who can do the same job, the station picks one, usually a close one, and tries not to overload any single helper.

sections.title: Loops, Jumps, Branches and Bidirectional Paths
sections.content:
An instance or SFF can change the SI or SPI to alter the route. Raising the SI is a loop back to an earlier function, lowering it by more than usual is a jump forward, and changing the SPI is a branch onto another path. The NSH has no marker showing whether a packet has already looped, so NSH metadata may be needed to prevent infinite loops.

Protocol control uses a special SFT value, Change Sequence. For it, each 8-octet entry in the list encodes a 3-byte SPI, a 1-byte SI and 4 reserved bytes. The SFF compares them with the current path to tell a loop, jump or branch. Special-purpose SFT values MUST NOT be advertised in SFIRs.

Because NSH packets carry no direction indicator, each direction of a bidirectional path needs its own SPI. An Association TLV with Association Type 1 links two unidirectional SFPRs into a bidirectional pair, and either path stays usable alone if its partner is missing. For stateful functions such as firewalls, the controller can build more specific SFPs so the classifier decides which instance a flow uses, at the cost of more SFP state.

The RFC also defines a Flow Specification action extended community (value 0x0d) so a controller can tell classifiers which SPI, SI and SFT to use for a flow, and an SPI/SI Representation Sub-TLV that lets the SPI and SI be carried as MPLS labels instead of an NSH.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a package should go back to an earlier stop, skip ahead, or switch to a different trip. The stop's helper can rewrite the numbers to make that happen.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanisms use BGP for the control plane, so techniques for authenticating BGP sessions help make it harder to spoof updates that could install bogus SFPs or advertise false SIs. The RFC says it does not fundamentally change BGP's security behavior, and that scoping to a single domain lets an operator decide on security measures more consistently.

Service function chaining already offers an attack opportunity: packets can be diverted, made to execute unexpected functions, or functions can be subverted. A control plane adds an attack vector, so the security of the BGP system is critical. The RFC points to the guidance in RFC 4364 for VPN-style routes, and stresses securely distinguishing messages for different overlays.

Where rogue controllers are a concern, it is RECOMMENDED that each SFF and classifier be configured with the identities of authorized controllers so SFPRs from other peers are rejected. Other communication between controllers and elements, such as binding functions to an SFF, is out of scope but is also an attack vector.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster sends fake trip lists, packages could go to the wrong places. So the stations should only trust lists from guides they know.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned address family number 31 and SAFI 9, both called "BGP SFC", and BGP path attribute 37, "SFP attribute". It created registries for SFP Attribute TLVs (initial entries 1 to 5), SFP Association Types (type 1, Bidirectional SFP), Service Function Types, SFC Extended Community Sub-Types and SPI/SI Representation Flags.

The Service Function Types registry reserves 0 and 65535, assigns 1 to 31 by Standards Action as special-purpose values, 32 to 64495 First Come First Served, and 64496 to 65534 for Private Use.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the official list of numbers. This RFC got new numbers added so everyone uses the same codes for these new kinds of notes.

items.label: Association TLV
items.desc: Links this SFPR to another SFP, for example to form a bidirectional pair.

items.label: Hop TLV
items.desc: One per hop: a Service Index plus Sub-TLVs.

items.desc: A Service Function Type and the instances allowed at the hop.

items.desc: Zero-length Sub-TLV for MPLS label-based hops.
